doc.title: Milt Fillius interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 18, 2000

title: The David Berger project and funding that fell through
summary: Berger's plan to document Milt Hinton's life led Fillius to engineer a grant, with complications over where to hold it.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans
story.community_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work

blocks.x: and he said I have an idea I want to do Milt’s life, and all his old friends and so on. And he said I’m going to apply to the National —

Endowment for the Arts, for the money but I may come short. Can you help me. I said sure. I said how much you talking about? He said well probably $50,000. I said yeah I can do that. So a year passed. Dizzy Gillespie died. That triggered it. So I called and said where the hell is the thing? I said here Dizzy’s gone and that’s one of the key guys you know, Milt and Dizzy were friends. And he said well they wouldn’t fund it. And I said well why didn’t you tell me? I said maybe I can. So he came up with a number, I don’t know, 250, 300, something like that, and applied to the foundation, and I engineered a grant. We had a problem in that we had to give the grant to an IRS-cleared institution. And the only one he had was Temple University. And he said I don’t trust those people. He taught there. He says I don’t trust those people. I said well maybe I know a place where we can put the money and they’ll dish it out as you need it. So I took the thing and Gene Tobin was in, and incidentally, in between was this conversation with Milt and Joe. That’s what really got me triggered with the thing. And I gave Gene the grant request and had him read it on the red eye coming back here, and he thought it was great for historic purposes. Because Gene’s been wonderful throughout this. And so he called and I said okay, I got a hold of Berger and I said Hamilton College will do it. We’ll put the money in trust at Hamilton College and as you need it you bill them and withdraw. So we started that. And then we tried to make an arrangement with Berger and it turned out that he was after a lot of dough and it just wasn’t the right thing. And then we said well let’s have Hamilton do it. We got the money. Well they had returned the money but I got it back again. And Joe Anderson and another alumnus rigged up a deal to do it, it didn’t make any sense. So we canceled that and then —
